newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.S. tries to negotiate North Iraq fighting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tries to negotiate North Iraq fighting.

text.p: A senior U.S. official trying to negotiate a ceasefire between warring Kurdish factions in northern Iraq was expected on Tuesday to meet Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani.

The meeting in Ankara with Robert Pelletreau, U.S. assistant secretary of state for near eastern affairs, comes as Talabani's Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) has retaken some territory lost last week to the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).
The KDP, headed by Massoud Barzani, on Monday fled an advance by the PUK, withdrawing in panic from the town of Ranya, which it had captured at the weekend.
Thousands of KDP fighters also abandoned an assault on a strategic dam when they came under heavy artillery fire from the PUK.

Pelletreau met KDP leader Barzani just over the border in Turkey on Monday as the United States tried to restart peace talks between the warring factions and prevent Baghdad or Tehran filling a power vacuum caused by the chaos.
Pelletreau said Barzani looked positively on a U.S.-proposed ceasefire with Talabani's PUK to "permit stability in the area for establishing an end to the fighting".

He warned against any military involvement by Iran or Iraq in the fighting. In late August Barzani got backing from Iraqi troops and tanks to take the main regional city of Arbil, which the PUK had held since a joint-administration collapsed in 1994.

"The United States would regard that as a negative development that could have very negative consequences," he told reporters after meeting Barzani for more than three hours at a Turkish military base in the border town of Silopi.

Fighting between the two factions since August has allowed Iraqi President Saddam Hussein to restore some of his influence in northern Iraq and end U.S. military, aid and intelligence presence in the mountainous region.
Barzani's decision to call on Baghdad -- which he has threatened to do again -- prompted U.S. missile strikes on military targets in southern Iraq in reprisal.
Barzani has accused Talabani of receiving military aid from Iran. Tehran and Talabani deny the charge.
There has been no obvious sign of Iranian or Iraqi forces in clashes this week.

The Kurds broke from Baghdad at the end of the 1991 Gulf War under Western protection and set up a power-sharing parliament in Arbil. That deal essentially collapsed in 1994 when Talabani's forces took control of the city.
